items.note: canonical AI self-help compound; documented in genre-slop.md as a cluster anchor phrase

items.note: documented in genre-slop.md as 'canonical AI motivational phrase'; the unlock metaphor applied to personhood
items.example: This program will help you unlock your potential.

items.note: intensified variant of the above; 'true' adds no content
items.example: Stop holding back and unlock your true potential.

items.note: target phrase; zero specificity, infinite self-congratulation
items.example: Follow these five habits to live your best life.

items.note: target phrase; originated in sports, now a hollow patience directive with no actionable content; FP risk in genuine athletic or process-management contexts
items.example: When things feel hard, just trust the process.

items.note: target phrase; gaming metaphor applied to personal development as a vague improvement verb; FP risk in actual game-design contexts
items.example: It's time to level up your mindset.

items.note: target phrase; posits a superior self-version without specifying what it means
items.example: These morning routines will help you become your best self.

items.note: target phrase; mystical-sounding phrase for internal motivation with no specifics
items.example: You already have the power within to change your life.

items.note: possessive variant of the journey cluster; FP risk in literal memoir or travel contexts
items.example: Honor your personal journey, wherever it takes you.

items.note: stacked cliche combining journey + self-discovery; genre-slop.md flags this exact phrase
items.example: Begin this journey of self-discovery with an open heart.

items.text: step out of your comfort zone
items.note: near-universal AI self-help phrase; documented in genre-slop.md as a cluster entry
items.example: Growth only happens when you step out of your comfort zone.

items.note: generic growth directive; variation on comfort-zone cluster
items.example: Every day is a chance to push past your limits.

items.note: forceful variant of the comfort-zone cluster; 'limitations' is vague by design
items.example: This mindset shift will help you break free from your limitations.

items.note: platitude with no actionable content; FP risk is high in isolation but low in density with other self-help phrases
items.example: The most important thing you can do is believe in yourself.

items.text: you are capable of more than you think
items.note: false-intimacy address; unfounded claim dressed as encouragement
items.example: You are capable of more than you think - start today.

items.note: empowerment formula opener; hollow unless completed with a specific action
items.example: You have the power to change your circumstances.

items.note: affirmation formula; assertive but content-free
items.example: No matter what others say, you are enough.

items.note: unconditional positive regard formula; applies to every human by default, says nothing
items.example: You deserve to be happy and fulfilled.

items.note: generic outcome promise attached to any self-help product or practice
items.example: These five habits can transform your life in 30 days.

items.note: generic directive; FP risk in genuine change-management writing, but usually a hollow imperative
items.example: The key to success is learning to embrace change.

items.note: hollow affirmation; 'who you are' is unspecified by design
items.example: Stop trying to be someone else and embrace who you are.

items.note: embrace + potential compound; documented in genre-slop.md as a cluster entry
items.example: It's time to embrace your potential and stop playing small.

items.note: synonym cycling on 'unlock your potential'; documented in genre-slop.md
items.example: Meditation helps you tap into your potential.

items.note: forceful variant of unlock/tap-into cluster; genre-slop.md flags this exact phrase
items.example: Stop shrinking yourself - unleash your potential.

items.note: adjective inflation applied to any event; FP risk in genuine program/retreat descriptions
items.example: This retreat was truly a transformative experience.

items.note: noun-phrase variant attaching transformation to any practice
items.example: Discover the transformative power of journaling.

items.note: genre-slop.md flags this as a 'philosophical platitude with zero evidence'
items.example: Even when things go wrong, remember that everything happens for a reason.

items.note: reductive advice that dismisses complexity; genre-slop.md flags this exact phrase
items.example: No matter what you're going through, just stay positive.

items.note: 'journey' slop applied specifically to health, from genre-slop.md medical/health section
items.example: Start your wellness journey with these daily habits.

items.note: Dweck's term now stripped of meaning; used as a hollow badge rather than a description of specific cognitive habits; FP risk in genuine educational/psychological writing
items.example: Developing a growth mindset is the key to success.

items.note: therapy-speak platitude meaning nothing more specific than 'try'; no concrete action
items.example: Every day is an opportunity to show up for yourself.

items.note: vague directive posing as insight; 'the work' is never specified; FP risk when 'the work' refers to a named process
items.example: There are no shortcuts - you have to do the work.

items.note: variant of 'do the work'; same hollow directive pattern
items.example: If you want results, you have to put in the work.

items.note: wellness-adjacent platitude; 'intention' here means nothing operational
items.example: When you live with intention, everything changes.

items.note: wellness ritual language used as a vague action directive
items.example: Every morning, take five minutes to set your intentions.

items.note: law-of-attraction language presenting visualization as a causal mechanism
items.example: You have the ability to manifest your dreams into reality.

items.note: wellness directive that has become hollow through repetition; FP risk when discussing actual gratitude research or practices with specifics
items.example: The simplest way to find joy is to practice gratitude.

items.note: mindfulness shorthand deployed as a complete answer to complex problems
items.example: The secret to happiness is simple: be present.

items.note: goal-setting directive assuming purpose is singular and findable; no method given
items.example: This course will help you find your purpose.

items.note: follow-on to 'find your purpose'; equally hollow
items.example: Once you find it, you have to live your purpose every day.

items.note: posits a hidden true identity distinct from the presented self; no mechanism for locating it
items.example: Be brave enough to show up as your authentic self.

items.note: variant of authentic-self cluster; tautological imperative
items.example: Stop performing for others and be authentically you.

items.note: vague psychological state deployed as a universal goal without description; FP risk in genuine meditation or clinical contexts
items.example: Follow these steps to achieve lasting inner peace.

items.note: genre-slop.md flags 'take control of your health today' as a motivational filler with zero specificity
items.example: It's never too late to take control of your health.

items.text: small changes can make a big difference
items.note: genre-slop.md flags this exact phrase as an empty platitude in health content
items.example: Don't be overwhelmed - small changes can make a big difference.

items.note: genre-slop.md flags this as a 'vague directive masquerading as advice'; FP risk is slightly higher in clinical/athletic contexts where it means something specific
items.example: The most important health skill you can develop is to listen to your body.

items.note: variant of 'your best self'; posits a superior self-iteration without specifying it
items.example: Commit to becoming your best version.

items.note: intensifier with no specifics; applied to any product, habit, or insight; FP risk is moderate since humans use it too
items.example: This book is absolutely life-changing.

items.note: cheerleader affirmation with zero informational content; appears constantly in AI self-help closers
items.example: It won't be easy, but you've got this.

items.note: genre-slop.md flags this as 'empty reassurance'; content-free
items.example: Whatever you're facing right now, you'll get through this.

items.note: journey metaphor as a call-to-action; completely generic
items.example: Ready to start your journey toward a better life?

items.note: journey metaphor used as filler to describe any ongoing process; FP risk in literal travel contexts
items.example: I hope these tips serve you well on your journey.

items.note: values-alignment language that presupposes articulated values without prompting the reader to specify them
items.example: Make decisions that align with your values.

items.note: agency-assertion formula; implies life is fully authored by individual will
items.example: You have everything you need to create the life you want.

items.note: entitlement framing used to replace effort instructions; applies universally, says nothing
items.example: You deserve success - stop letting fear hold you back.

items.note: scarcity vs. abundance framing from Covey/New-Age tradition; now a hollow badge in self-help content
items.example: Shift from a scarcity mindset to an abundance mindset.

items.note: spiritual-self framework used as shorthand for aspiration; no operational meaning
items.example: Meditation connects you to your higher self.

items.note: therapy-adjacent term now used as a vague label for any self-reflection activity; FP risk in genuine therapeutic writing
items.example: Real change requires doing the inner work.

items.note: therapeutic frame applied to abstract nouns (money, food, time) as a generic reframing hook; FP risk when referring to actual relationships
items.example: It's time to heal your relationship with food.

items.note: empowerment formula implying power was taken, now recoverable through the advice offered; no mechanism given
items.example: Stop giving away your energy and reclaim your power.

items.note: self-improvement framing that conflates personal development with financial logic; used to justify any purchase or practice; FP risk is moderate since the phrase has genuine uses
items.example: The best investment you can make is to invest in yourself.

items.note: survive/thrive contrast template; formulaic binary with no specifics on what thriving means
items.example: You deserve to thrive, not just survive.

items.note: narrative-self empowerment formula; vague action directive
items.example: The first step to healing is learning to own your story.

items.note: relativistic framing that treats personal perspective as unquestionable fact; 'speak your truth' is the fuller form
items.example: Don't be afraid to speak your truth.

items.note: Gandhi misquote recycled as a hollow imperative in self-help and marketing copy
items.example: If you want to see a better world, be the change.

items.note: 'radical' used as an intensifier to distinguish from ordinary self-acceptance; the modifier adds no specific meaning
items.example: The path forward starts with radical self-love.

items.note: formulaic rebuttal to a strawman; the sentence structure signals the genre
items.example: Remember: self-care is not selfish.

items.note: emotional-validation directive that validates without guiding; FP risk in genuine therapeutic writing
items.example: Allow yourself to honor your feelings without judgment.

items.text: life is a journey, not a destination
items.note: genre-slop.md flags this exact phrase as a 'not X, it's Y aphorism with zero content'
items.example: As the saying goes, life is a journey, not a destination.

items.text: not a destination but a journey
items.note: reversed variant of the above; same zero-content aphorism
items.example: Success is not a destination but a journey.

items.note: motivational platitude implying all starting points are equivalent; typically precedes a call-to-action
items.example: You don't need to be ready. Just start where you are.

items.note: extended form of 'your best self'; product-sales framing of personal development
items.example: This program is designed to help you become the best version of yourself.

items.note: empowerment-action metaphor that implies power is a space one can physically enter; no mechanism given
items.example: This workshop is about stepping into your power.

items.text: where you are meant to be
items.note: deterministic framing used to validate any current state; unfalsifiable
items.example: Trust that you are exactly where you are meant to be.

items.text: you are exactly where you need to be
items.note: validation formula that accepts the status quo as correct by assertion; common in AI-generated affirmation content
items.example: Stop rushing. You are exactly where you need to be.

items.note: self-prioritization directive; 'choose' is used intransitively, eliminating the need to specify what the choice entails
items.example: Stop waiting for others to pick you. Choose yourself.

items.note: container-self metaphor for self-investment; deliberately vague about what 'pouring' means
items.example: You can't pour from an empty cup - pour into yourself first.

items.text: you can't pour from an empty cup
items.note: justification-for-self-care metaphor in cliche form; common in wellness and coaching content
items.example: You can't pour from an empty cup, so take care of yourself first.

items.note: empowerment directive originating in feminist discourse, now a hollow affirmation deployed generically; FP risk in genuine discussions of social space-claiming
items.example: You have every right to take up space in this world.

items.note: variant of 'inner work'; the 'do' form appears as a complete directive without specifying the work
items.example: Change starts when you commit to do the inner work.
